stanzas: At sa kaniyáng yumi at ganda,
Love, which was in her palm,
And by her grace and beauty
My country, you were taken captive,
Even a bird that is free to fly,
How much more a country, so splendid,
that would not long to break free?
nest of my tears and misery,

notes: line 1.3: 'palad' is the palm of the hand and also one's lot or fate; 'Pag-ibig ang sa kaniyang palad' can read 'Love was in her palm' or 'Love was her lot'. The sense of 1.3-4: love, which she held (or which was her destiny), gave her beauty and splendour.
line 1.4 and 2.3: 'dilag' is radiance, splendour; 'sakdal-dilag' (2.3) is 'perfectly splendid'.
line 2.3-4: one rhetorical question: if even a bird weeps when caged, how much more a country; 'Bayan pa kaya' is 'how much more, then, a country'.
line 2.5: 'minumutya' is from 'mutya', a pearl or treasure: 'whom I cherish as a pearl'.

Source metadata: the import puts José Corazón de Jesús in the 'translator' field; he wrote these Tagalog words (1929) to Constancio de Guzmán's music, so he is the author of the text, not a translator.
